### 1.2 Related Work

Control of Dynamical Systems: Control theory, grounded in deep mathematical foundations and with a long history of practical applications, dates back to self-regulating feedback mechanisms in ancient Greece. The first formal mathematical treatment is attributed to James Clerk Maxwell (Maxwell, 1868). For a historical perspective, see Fernández Cara and Zuazua Iriondo (2003). The problem of stabilizing general dynamical systems has been shown to be NP-hard (Ahmadi, 2016); see Blondel and Tsitsiklis (2000) for a comprehensive survey on the computational complexity of control.

Linear Dynamical Systems: Even simple questions about general dynamical systems are intractable. In control, Lyapunov pioneered the use of linearization to analyze local stability of nonlinear systems (Lyapunov, 1992). The seminal work of Kalman (1960) introduced state-space methods and showed that any LDS can be controlled under stochastic assumptions and known quadratic costs.

Online Stochastic Control: Early work in the ML community on control focused on the online LQR setting (Abbasi-Yadkori and Szepesvári, 2011; Dean et al., 2018; Mania et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2019), achieving $\sqrt{T}$ regret with polynomial runtime. A parallel line of work (Cohen et al., 2018) studied online LQR with adversarially chosen quadratic losses, also achieving $\sqrt{T}$ regret. In all of these works, regret is measured against the best linear controller in hindsight.

Online Nonstochastic Control: Recent methods for fully adversarial control are surveyed in Hazan and Singh (2025). These approaches typically learn a parameterized mapping from past disturbances to control inputs, with the number of parameters—and hence the runtime—scaling polynomially with the inverse of the stability margin. Our work builds on the setting of Agarwal et al. (2019a), proposing a more efficient algorithm with similar regret guarantees.

Subsequent work has refined the regret bounds under additional assumptions. Agarwal et al. (2019b) established logarithmic regret for strongly convex costs in the presence of stochastic or semi-adversarial noise, while Foster and Simchowitz (2020) derived similar guarantees for known quadratic costs under fully adversarial noise.

Beyond the full-information setting, Simchowitz et al. (2020) extended the framework to partial observation, Minasyan et al. (2022) analyzed adaptive regret in unknown and time-varying systems, and Sun et al. (2023); Suggala et al. (2024) studied online control with bandit feedback.

Online control has also seen applications in diverse domains, including mechanical ventilation (Suo et al., 2022), meta-optimization (Chen and Hazan, 2023), and the regulation of population dynamics (Golowich et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025).

Online Convex Optimization: Our method reduces online control to online convex optimization. For background on regret minimization and online learning, see Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi (2006); Hazan (2016).

Learning in Linear Dynamical Systems: Hardt et al. (2016) showed that unknown linear dynamical systems (LDSs) can be learned by applying random Gaussian inputs and optimizing via gradient descent. This approach was later extended to higher-dimensional and marginally stable systems by Sarkar and Rakhlin (2019). More recently, Bakshi et al. (2023a) introduced tensor-based methods for learning LDSs, and Bakshi et al. (2023b) extended these techniques to handle mixtures of LDSs, following the formulation of Chen and Poor (2022). While these tensor-based approaches avoid dependence on the system’s condition number, their computational complexity still scales with the hidden dimension—a limitation addressed by recent developments in spectral filtering.

Spectral Filtering: Spectral filtering was originally introduced for sequence prediction in online learning, as a means of bypassing the non-convexity inherent in learning linear dynamical systems (Hazan et al., 2017; Agarwal et al., 2024b). Hazan et al. (2018) extended the method to systems with non-symmetric dynamics, though their analysis incurred a dependence on the hidden dimension. This limitation was subsequently addressed by Marsden and Hazan (2025), who incorporated autoregressive structure and used Chebyshev polynomial approximations to obtain dimension-free bounds.

While spectral filtering has proven effective in prediction settings, its application to control remains limited. To our knowledge, the only prior use is by Arora et al. (2018), who applied spectral filtering as a black-box subroutine in the offline LQR setting with unknown dynamics. In contrast, we address the online control problem, and develop a new spectral filtering approach applicable to any controllable system (Definition 3.1), competing with the best diagonalizably stable policy in hindsight (Definition 3.4).

The key technical difference is that, unlike in prediction settings where past responses are available, online control requires leveraging system stability and integrating over a different set of eigenvalues, resulting in a distinct Hankel structure (see (2.1)).

## 2 Algorithm and Main Result

Our approach employs a convex relaxation of the linear control problem by computing universal spectral filters and then learning a linear combination of the multiplication of past disturbances with these filters, as described in detail in Algorithm 1. The spectral filters are universal in the sense that they are independent of the specific linear dynamical system (LDS) at hand, the initial state, the disturbances, and the cost functions. In fact, they correspond exactly to the top eigenvectors of the matrix $H\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ for some memory $m$ , whose entries are given by

$$ \displaystyle H_{ij}=\frac{(1-\gamma)^{i+j-1}}{i+j-1}, $$

where $\gamma$ is an assumed bound on the system’s instability margin, formally defined in Definition 3.4. We illustrate the filters in Figure 1. The number of required eigenvectors, denoted by $h$ , also determines the number of learnable parameters.

*Figure 1: Entries of the first six eigenvectors of $H_{500}$ , plotted coordinate-wise.*

*Algorithm 1 Online Spectral Control Algorithm*

```
1: Input: Horizon $T$ , number of parameters $h$ , memory $m$ , step size $\eta$ , convex constrains set ${\mathcal{K}}\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{h\times n\times d}$ .
2: Compute $\{(\sigma_{j},\bm{\phi}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{h}$ , the top $h$ eigenpairs of $H$ from Eq. (2.1).
3: Initialize $M_{1:h}^{0}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{h\times n\times d}$ .
4: for $t=0,\ldots,T-1$ do
5: Define $\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}=[\mathbf{w}_{t-1},\dots,\mathbf{w}_{t-m}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$
6: Compute control $\mathbf{u}_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{h}\sigma_{i}^{1/4}M_{i}^{t}\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\bm{\phi}_{i}$
7: Observe the new state $\mathbf{x}_{t+1}$ and record $\mathbf{w}_{t}=\mathbf{x}_{t+1}-A\mathbf{x}_{t}-B\mathbf{u}_{t}$ .
8: Set $M^{t+1}_{1:h}=\Pi_{{\mathcal{K}}}\left[M^{t}_{1:h}-\eta\nabla_{M}\ell_{t}\left(M^{t}_{1:h}\right)\right]$
9: end for
10: return $M^{T}_{1:h}$
```

### 2.1 Algorithm

In Algorithm 1 we learn a mapping from disturbances $\mathbf{w}_{t}$ to controllers $\mathbf{u}_{t}$ . However, instead of learning a linear mapping of the disturbances, we learn a linear mapping of a specific matrix product involving the disturbances and the filters. Notably, in line 7 we explicitly leverage our knowledge of the system to compute the disturbances from the observed state and the chosen controller.

Finally, Algorithm 1 is simply an instance of Projected Online Gradient Descent (Zinkevich, 2003), applied to some convex set ${\mathcal{K}}$ in which each element is a sequence of $h$ matrices from ${\mathbb{R}}^{n\times d}$ , and the loss functions are the specific memory-less loss functions $\ell_{t}$ , as in Definition 4.4.

### 2.2 Main Result

While we defer the formalization of our assumptions and notations to Section 3, we present our main result here:

#### Theorem 2.1 (Main Theorem).

Let $c_{t}$ be any sequence of convex Lipschitz cost functions satisfying Assumption 3.3, and let the LDS be controllable (Definition 3.1) and satisfy Assumption 3.2. Then, Algorithm 1 achieves the following regret bound:

$$ \text{Regret}_{T}\left(\mathrm{OSC},\mathcal{S}\right)=\frac{C_{0}C_{1}\sqrt{T}}{\gamma^{4}}\log^{3}\left(\frac{C_{1}Td}{\gamma^{3}}\right)\,, $$

where $\mathcal{S}$ is the class of linear policies defined in Definition 3.4. This result holds under the following choice of inputs:

- (i) $m=\left\lceil\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{8C_{1}\sqrt{T}}{\gamma^{3}}\right)\right\rceil$ ,

- (ii) $h=\left\lceil 4\log T\log\left(\frac{900C_{1}dT}{\gamma^{3}}\right)\right\rceil$ ,

- (iii) $\eta=C_{2}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma^{3}}{Tmh}}$ ,

- (iv) $K$ is the set from Definition 4.2,

where the constants are defined as follows:

$$ \displaystyle C_{0}\leq 10^{3}\,,\quad C_{1}=G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}\,,\quad C_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\kappa^{5}}{3C_{1}}\,. $$

Note that Algorithm 1 maintains at most $h=O\left(\mathrm{polylog}\left(T/\gamma\right)\right)$ parameters at each step $t$ . Moreover, the matrix multiplications between $\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}$ and $\bm{\phi}_{i}$ (in line 6 of Algorithm 1) for each time step $t\in[T]$ , can be computed by zero-padding $\bm{\phi}_{i}$ to be $T$ -dimensional and performing online convolution with the disturbance stream $\{\mathbf{w}_{t}\}_{t\in[T]}$ . Using the efficient online convolution technique introduced in Agarwal et al. (2024a) for this task, we obtain the following corollary:

#### Corollary 2.2.

The average running time of each of the $T$ executions of the inner loop in Algorithm 1 is $O\left(\log^{4}\left(T/\gamma\right)\right)$ .

#### Proof Roadmap.

The proof of Theorem 2.1 follows a two-step strategy. First, we show that the class of diagonalizably stable linear policies can be approximated by a family of spectral controllers with bounded parameters (Lemma 4.3). Second, we analyze the regret of Algorithm 1, which performs projected online gradient descent over this spectral policy class. The analysis leverages convexity of the loss functions and boundedness of the feasible set. A high-level overview of the analysis appears in Section 4, and full proofs are provided in Sections 5–8.

## 3 Preliminaries

### 3.1 Notation

We use $\mathbf{x}$ to denote states, $\mathbf{u}$ for control inputs, and $\mathbf{w}$ for disturbances. The dimensions of the state and control spaces are denoted by $d=\dim(\mathbf{x})$ and $n=\dim(\mathbf{u})$ , respectively. Matrices related to the system dynamics and control policy are denoted by capital letters $A,B,K,M$ . For convenience, we write $\mathbf{w}_{t}=0$ for all $t<0$ .

For any $t_{2}\geq t_{1}$ , we define $\tilde{W}_{t_{2}:t_{1}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times(t_{2}-t_{1}+1)}$ as the matrix whose columns are $\mathbf{w}_{t_{2}},\dots,\mathbf{w}_{t_{1}}$ , in that order. Additionally, given matrices $M_{1},\dots,M_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ , we define $M_{1:h}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d\times h}$ as their concatenation along the third dimension.

Given a policy $\pi$ , we denote the state and control at time $t$ by $(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\pi},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{\pi})$ when following $\pi$ . If $\pi$ is parameterized by a set of parameters $\Theta$ , and the context makes the inputs clear, we use $(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\Theta},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{\Theta})$ or $(\mathbf{x}_{t}(\Theta),\mathbf{u}_{t}(\Theta))$ to refer to the same quantities. For simplicity, we use $(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})$ without any superscript or argument to refer to the state and control at time $t$ under Algorithm 1.

### 3.2 Setting

We now present the key definitions and outline the assumptions used throughout the paper. Our setting considers adversarial noise and convex cost functions. We begin by defining controllability:

#### Definition 3.1.

An LDS as in (1.1) is controllable if the noiseless LDS given by $\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=A\mathbf{x}_{t}+B\mathbf{u}_{t}$ can be steered to any target state from any initial state.

Since the disturbances are non-stochastic, we assume without loss of generality that $\mathbf{x}_{0}=0$ . The following assumptions formalize the notions of bounded disturbances and Lipschitz continuity of cost functions over bounded domains.

#### Assumption 3.2.

The system matrix $B$ is bounded, i.e., $\|B\|\leq\kappa_{B}$ . The disturbance at each time step is also bounded, i.e., $\|\mathbf{w}_{t}\|\leq W$ .

#### Assumption 3.3.

The cost functions $c_{t}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u})$ are convex. Moreover, as long as $\|\mathbf{x}\|,\|\mathbf{u}\|\leq D$ , the gradients are bounded:

$$ \|\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}c_{t}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u})\|,\|\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}c_{t}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u})\|\leq GD\,. $$

In Definition 3.1 of Cohen et al. (2018), the notion of a $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -strongly stable linear policy is introduced. Since our spectral analysis focuses on diagonalization, in Definition 3.4, we extend this to the notion of $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -diagonalizably stable policies.:

#### Definition 3.4.

A linear policy $K$ is $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -diagonalizably stable if there exist matrices $L,H$ satisfying $A+BK=HLH^{-1}$ , such that the following conditions hold:

- 1. $L$ is diagonal with nonnegative entries.

- 2. The spectral norm of $L$ is strictly less than one, i.e., $\|L\|\leq 1-\gamma$ .

- 3. The controller and the transformation matrices are bounded, i.e., $\|K\|,\|H\|,\|H^{-1}\|\leq\kappa$ .

We denote by $\mathcal{S}=\{K:K\text{ is }(\kappa,\gamma)\text{-diagonalizably stable}\}$ the set of such policies, and, with slight abuse of notation, also use $\mathcal{S}$ to refer to the class of linear policies $\mathbf{u}_{t}=S\mathbf{x}_{t}$ where $S\in\mathcal{S}$ . Each policy in $\mathcal{S}$ is fully parameterized by the matrix $K\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times d}$ .

Definition 3.4 is similar to diagonal strong stability (Definition 2.3 of Agarwal et al. (2019b)), with the key difference that we require $L$ to have real eigenvalues.11 1 The requirement of nonnegative eigenvalues can be relaxed by integrating over a larger set; it is imposed here for ease of presentation. Note that by Ackermann’s formula (Ackermann, 1972; Galiaskarov et al., 2023), there always exists $K\in\mathcal{S}$ that controls the noiseless system. Finally, we introduce the following assumption for clarity of presentation, which we later relax in Section 8.

#### Assumption 3.5.

The zero policy $K=0$ lies in $\mathcal{S}$ .22 2 Assumption 3.5 can be relaxed via a simple reduction, as outlined in Section 8. Theorem 2.1 holds without this assumption, up to an additional factor of $\kappa$ in $C_{1}$ .

For simplicity, we assume that $\kappa,\kappa_{B},W\geq 1$ and $\gamma\leq 2/3$ , without loss of generality.

## 4 Analysis Overview

We present the proof of our main result here, while deferring the proofs of technical lemmas to the following sections. Before proceeding, we outline the key technical considerations involved in establishing our final regret bound.

Algorithm 1 learns a convex relaxation of the policy class $\mathcal{S}$ , referred to as the spectral policy class, defined as follows:

#### Definition 4.1.

[Spectral Controller] The class of Spectral Controllers with $h$ parameters, memory $m$ and stability $\gamma$ is defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\Pi^{\sf SC}_{h,m,\gamma}=\left\{\pi_{h,m,\gamma,M}^{\sf SC}(\mathbf{w}_{t-1:t-m})=\sum_{i=1}^{h}\sigma_{i}^{1/4}M_{i}\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\bm{\phi}_{i}\right\}\,, $$

where $\bm{\phi}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m},\sigma_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}$ are the $i^{\sf th}$ top eigenvector and eigenvalue of $H\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m\times m}$ such that $H_{ij}=\frac{\left(1-\gamma\right)^{i+j-1}}{i+j-1}$ . Any policy in this class is fully parameterized by the matrices $M_{1:h}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times d\times h}$ .

To enable learning via online gradient descent, we require a bounded set of parameters:

#### Definition 4.2.

The set of bounded spectral parameters is defined as

$$ {\mathcal{K}}=\left\{M_{1:h}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{h\times n\times d}\mid\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M}\right\rVert\leq\frac{3\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma},\left\lVert M_{1:h}\right\rVert\leq\kappa^{3}\sqrt{\frac{2h}{\gamma}}\right\}\,. $$

In Section 5, we prove that the spectral policy class can approximate $\mathcal{S}$ up to arbitrary accuracy. Formally, we state this as:

#### Lemma 4.3.

For any linear policy $K\in\mathcal{S}$ , there exists a $\sf SC$ policy with $M\in{\mathcal{K}}$ such that for any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ :

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K})\right|\leq\varepsilon T\,, $$

if (i) $m=\left\lceil\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{8C_{1}}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\right)\right\rceil$ and (ii) $h\geq 2\log T\log\left(\frac{900C_{1}d}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\log^{1/2}\left(\frac{8C_{1}}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\right)\right)$ where $C_{1}$ is as defined in Theorem 2.1.

We further note that in Algorithm 1, online gradient descent is not performed on the actual cost function, but on a modified cost function, referred to as the memory-less loss function:

#### Definition 4.4.

We define the memory-less loss function at time $t$ as

$$ \displaystyle\ell_{t}(M_{1:h})=c_{t}({\mathbf{x}_{t}\left(M_{1:h}\right)},{\mathbf{u}_{t}\left(M_{1:h}\right)})\,. $$

Classical results in online gradient descent provide a regret bound with respect to loss functions $\ell_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})$ . However, our regret is defined in terms of the actual costs $c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})$ . Nevertheless, in Section 6.3, we prove that $c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})$ is well approximated by $\ell_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})$ . We formally state this result as:

#### Lemma 4.5.

Algorithm 1 is executed with $\eta=C_{2}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma^{3}}{Tmh}}$ . Then for every $t\in[T]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})-\ell_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})\right|\leq\frac{6C_{1}\sqrt{mh}}{\gamma^{7/2}\sqrt{T}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\,, $$

where $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are as defined in Theorem 2.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 2.1.

For $\varepsilon=1/\sqrt{T}$ , observe that our choice of $m$ and $h$ satisfies the conditions in Lemma 4.3 (using the fact that $T,d,C\geq 1$ and $0<\gamma<1$ ). Hence, using Lemma 4.3 and the Definition 4.4 we get:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{M^{\star}\in{\mathcal{K}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(M^{\star}_{1:h})-\min_{K\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K})\leq\sqrt{T}\leq\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{T}}{\gamma^{4}}\log^{3}\left(\frac{C_{1}Td}{\gamma^{3}}\right)\,. $$

We now invoke the regret of the Online Gradient Descent, stated in Theorem 3.1 in Hazan (2016). By Lemma 6.1 the set ${\mathcal{K}}$ is convex, and by Lemma 6.2 the memory-less loss functions are convex functions. Furthermore, using the bound on lipschitz constant of the memory-less loss computed in Lemma 6.3 and the bound of the diameter of ${\mathcal{K}}$ , for our choice of $\eta$ , we get a regret bound. For our choice of $h$ and $m$ , the regret bound evaluates to:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}\left(M_{1:h}^{t}\right)-\min_{M^{\star}\in{\mathcal{K}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}\left(M_{1:h}^{\star}\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{384C_{1}\sqrt{T}}{\gamma^{4}}\log^{3}\left(\frac{900C_{1}dT}{\gamma^{3}}\right). $$

Next, Lemma 4.5 gives us the following bound on the difference between the memory-less loss $\ell_{t}(M^{t}_{1:h})$ and the cost incurred by the algorithm $c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})$ for every $t\in[T]$ . Taking the sum over all $t\in[T]$ :

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}\left({\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t}}\right)-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}\left(M_{1:h}^{t}\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{24C_{1}\sqrt{T}}{\gamma^{4}}\log^{3}\left(\frac{900C_{1}dT}{\gamma^{3}}\right)\,. $$

Finally, we add equations (4.2),(4.3),(4.4) together to obtain the result. ∎

## 5 Approximation Results

To prove Lemma 4.3, we shall show that the class of $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -diagonalizably stable linear policies can be approximated using Open-Loop Optimal Controllers (Definition 5.1) in Lemma 5.2. We then show that the class of open-loop optimal controllers can be approximated by the class of spectral controllers in Lemma 5.3. We begin by defining the class of open-loop optimal controllers as follows:

#### Definition 5.1 (Open Loop Optimal Controller).

The class of Open Loop Optimal Controllers of with memory $m$ is defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\Pi^{\sf OLOC}_{m}=\left\{\pi_{m,K}^{\sf OLOC}(\mathbf{w}_{t-1:t-m})=K\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(A+BK\right)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\right\}\,. $$

Any policy in this class is fully parameterized by the matrix $K\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times n}$ and the memory $m\in\mathbb{Z}$ .

Next, we state and prove Lemma 5.2, which shows that any linear policy in $\mathcal{S}$ can be approximated up to arbitrary accuracy with an open-loop optimal controller of suitable memory.

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let a linear policy $K\in\mathcal{S}$ . Then, for $m\geq\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{8G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\right)$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K})\right|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}T\,,\quad\quad\quad\quad\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq\frac{2\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}\,. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by bounding the difference in the state and the difference in the control inputs. The difference in cost is bounded using the fact that the cost functions are lipschitz in the control and state. We begin by unrolling the expressions for $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}$ in terms of $\mathbf{w}_{t}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}=K\sum_{i=1}^{t}(A+BK)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\,,\quad\quad\quad\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}=\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K}\,. $$

Notice that for all $t\leq m$ , $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}=\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}$ and hence $\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}=\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}$ . For $t>m$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert \displaystyle=\left\lVert K\sum_{i=1}^{t}(A+BK)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}-K\sum_{i=1}^{m}(A+BK)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\right\rVert \displaystyle=\left\lVert K\sum_{i=m+1}^{t}(A+BK)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq\kappa^{3}W\sum_{i=m+1}^{t}(1-\gamma)^{i-1} \displaystyle[\Delta-\mbox{ineq., C-S}] \displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}(1-\gamma)^{m}\,. $$

Using this together with (5.1) and the fact that $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}=\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}$ for any $t\leq m$ , we similarly get:

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B(\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K,m})\right\rVert=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t-m}A^{i-1}B(\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K,m})\right\rVert\,, $$

and by using Assumption 3.5 we can write:

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}(1-\gamma)^{i-1}\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq\frac{\kappa_{B}\kappa^{5}W}{\gamma^{2}}(1-\gamma)^{m}\,. $$

Using the fact that $\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}/\gamma>1$ , we get the following uniform bound:

$$ \displaystyle\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\right\}\leq\frac{\kappa_{B}\kappa^{5}W}{\gamma^{2}}(1-\gamma)^{m}\,. $$

Whenever $m\geq\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}}{\gamma}\right)$ , which is indeed true from our choice of $\varepsilon$ and $m$ , this implies that the $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq\kappa^{3}W/\gamma$ . Using Lemma 5.4 $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}\right\rVert\leq\kappa^{3}W/\gamma$ , by triangle inequality $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq 2\kappa^{3}W/\gamma$ . Thus, the sum of costs is bounded using lipschitzness of $c_{t}$ as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m})\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{2G\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert+\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{4G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}}{\gamma^{3}}(1-\gamma)^{m}\cdot T\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}T\,. \displaystyle[\mbox{choice of }m] $$

∎

We shall now prove that every open-loop optimal controller can be approximated up to arbitrary accuracy with a spectral controller.

#### Lemma 5.3.

For every open loop optimal controller $\pi_{K,m}^{\sf OLOC}$ such that $K\in\mathcal{S}$ and $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq 2\kappa^{3}W/\gamma$ , there exists an spectral controller $\pi_{h,m,\gamma,M}^{\sf SC}$ with $M\in{\mathcal{K}}$ such that:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m})\right|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}T\,. $$

for any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $h\geq 2\log T\log\left(\frac{600G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}\sqrt{m}d}{\varepsilon\gamma^{5/2}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\right)$ .

#### Proof.

Since $K\in\mathcal{S}$ , there exists a diagonal $L\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times n}$ as in Definition 3.4 so that:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m} \displaystyle=K\sum_{i=1}^{m}(A+BK)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}=K\sum_{i=1}^{m}HL^{i-1}H^{-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\,. $$

Then write $L^{i-1}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{j}^{i-1}e_{j}e_{j}^{\top}$ and obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}=K\sum_{i=1}^{m}H\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}\alpha_{j}^{i-1}e_{j}e_{j}^{\top}\right)H^{-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i} \displaystyle=K\sum_{j=1}^{d}He_{j}e_{j}^{\top}H^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{j}^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\,. $$

Recall $\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}=[\mathbf{w}_{t-1},\dots,\mathbf{w}_{t-m}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}$ , define $\bm{\mu}_{\alpha}=[1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{m-1}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$ and get

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m} \displaystyle=K\sum_{j=1}^{d}He_{j}e_{j}^{\top}H^{-1}\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{j}} \displaystyle=K\sum_{j=1}^{d}He_{j}e_{j}^{\top}H^{-1}\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{\phi}_{i}\bm{\phi}_{i}^{\top}\right)\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{j}} \displaystyle\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{\phi}_{i}\bm{\phi}_{i}^{\top}=\mathbb{I}_{m}\right] \displaystyle=K\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}He_{j}e_{j}^{\top}H^{-1}\bm{\phi}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{j}}\right)\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\bm{\phi}_{i}\,. $$

Let $\pi_{h,m,\gamma,M^{*}}^{\sf SC}$ be the spectral controller with $M^{*}_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{-1/4}KH\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bm{\phi}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{j}}e_{j}e_{j}^{\top}\right)H^{-1}$ for all $i\in[h]$ . Note that we have

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert M^{*}_{i}\right\rVert\leq\kappa^{3}\cdot\max_{\ell\in[d]}\sigma_{j}^{-1/4}\left<\bm{\phi}_{j},\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{l}}\right>\quad\forall 1\leq j\leq m\,, $$

and from the analysis of Lemma 7.4, we have that $\sigma_{j}^{-1/4}\left<\bm{\phi}_{j},\mu(\alpha_{l})\right>\leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{\gamma}}$ . Thus, $\left\lVert M^{*}_{1:h}\right\rVert\leq\kappa^{3}\sqrt{\frac{2h}{\gamma}}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}}\right\rVert \displaystyle=\left\lVert K\sum_{i=h+1}^{m}H\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bm{\phi}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{j}}e_{j}e_{j}^{\top}\right)H^{-1}\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\bm{\phi}_{i}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq\kappa^{3}W\sqrt{m}\sum_{i=h+1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{d}|\bm{\phi}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{j}}| \displaystyle\left[\left\lVert\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\right\rVert\leq W\sqrt{m}\right] \displaystyle\leq\frac{30\kappa^{3}W\sqrt{m}}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\sum_{i=h+1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\exp\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}j}{16\log T}\right) \displaystyle\left[\text{Lemma \ref{lem:in-prod-bound}}\right] \displaystyle\leq\frac{30\kappa^{3}W\sqrt{m}d}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\intop_{h}^{\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}j}{16\log T}\right)dx \displaystyle\leq\frac{50\kappa^{3}W\sqrt{m}d}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\exp\left({-\frac{\pi^{2}h}{16\log T}}\right)\,, $$

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M^{*}}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert \displaystyle=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B(\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{M^{*}}-\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K,m})\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{t}(1-\gamma)^{i-1}\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{M}-\mathbf{u}_{t-i}^{K,m}\right\rVert \displaystyle[\mbox{Assumption \ref{asm:zero-stabilizable-system}}] \displaystyle\leq\frac{50\kappa_{B}\kappa^{5}W\sqrt{m}d}{\gamma^{3/2}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\exp\left({-\frac{\pi^{2}h}{16\log T}}\right)\,. $$

Using the fact that $\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}/\gamma>1$ , we get a uniform bound:

$$ \displaystyle\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M^{*}}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}}\right\rVert\right\}\leq\frac{50\kappa_{B}\kappa^{5}W\sqrt{m}d}{\gamma^{3/2}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\exp\left({-\frac{\pi^{2}h}{16\log T}}\right)\,. $$

Whenever $h\geq 2\log T\log\left(\frac{50\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}\sqrt{m}d}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\log T\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\right)$ , which is indeed the case for our choice of $\varepsilon$ and $h$ , this implies that $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M^{*}}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq\kappa^{3}W/\gamma$ . Hence, by triangle inequality $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M^{*}}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}}\right\rVert\leq 3\kappa^{2}W/\gamma$ . Thus, the sum of costs is bounded as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M^{*}},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m})\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{3G\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M^{*}}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert+\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{300G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}\sqrt{m}d}{\gamma^{5/2}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\exp\left({-\frac{\pi^{2}h}{16\log T}}\right)\cdot T \displaystyle\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}T\,.\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad[\mbox{choice of }h] $$

∎

We conclude the proof of Lemma 4.3 using Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3 as follows:

Proof of Lemma 4.3: $K$ is a $(\kappa,\gamma)-$ diagonalizably stable linear policy and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ . Hence, by Lemma 5.2, for the choice of $m=\left\lceil\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{8G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\right)\right\rceil$ , we have that

$$ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K})\right|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}T\,,\quad\quad\quad\quad\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq\frac{2\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}\,. $$

Since $\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\leq\frac{2\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}$ , for any $h\geq 2\log T\log\left(\frac{600G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}\sqrt{m}d}{\varepsilon\gamma^{5/2}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\right)$ , there exists an $M\in{\mathcal{K}}$ such that:

$$ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m})\right|\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{2}T\,. $$

In particular, since $2x\geq\lceil x\rceil$ for $x>0.5$ and since $\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{8G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\right)\geq\log(8)>0.5$ , $m\leq\frac{2}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{8G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\right)$ . Thus, for $h\geq 2\log T\log\left(\frac{900G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}d}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\log T\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\log^{1/2}\left(\frac{8G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}}{\varepsilon\gamma^{3}}\right)\right)$ there exists such an $M\in{\mathcal{K}}$ . Using triangle inequality, we get:

$$ \sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K})\right|\leq\varepsilon T\,. $$

$\square$

Finally, we derive the bound on the state and control obtained by following a linear policy from $\mathcal{S}$ , which we use in the proof of Lemma 5.2.

#### Lemma 5.4.

For any $K\in\mathcal{S}$ , the corresponding states $\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}$ and control inputs $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}$ are bounded by

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{x}^{K}_{t}\right\rVert\leq\frac{\kappa^{2}W}{\gamma}\,,\quad\left\lVert\mathbf{u}^{K}_{t}\right\rVert\leq\frac{\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}\,. $$

#### Proof.

As in many other parts of this paper, we first write the states as a linear transformation of the disturbances:

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}\right\rVert \displaystyle=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left(A+BK\right)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=0}^{t}\left(1-\gamma\right)^{i}\left\lVert\mathbf{w}_{t-i-1}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq\frac{\kappa^{2}W}{\gamma}\,. $$

Then, since $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}=K\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}$ with $\left\lVert K\right\rVert\leq\kappa$ , we obtain the result. ∎

## 6 Learning Results

### 6.1 Convexity of loss function and feasibility set

To conclude the analysis, we first show that the feasibility set ${\mathcal{K}}$ is convex and the loss functions are convex with respect to the variables $M_{1:h}$ . This follows since the states and the controls are linear transformations of the variables.

#### Lemma 6.1.

The set ${\mathcal{K}}=\left\{M_{1:h}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{h\times n\times d}\mid\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M}\right\rVert\leq\frac{3\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma},\left\lVert M_{1:h}\right\rVert\leq\kappa^{3}\sqrt{\frac{2h}{\gamma}}\right\}$ is convex.

#### Proof.

Since $\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M},\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M}$ are linear in $M_{1:h}$ , from the convexity of the norm, the fact that the sublevel sets of a convex function is convex and that the intersection of convex sets is convex, we are done. ∎

#### Lemma 6.2.

The loss $\ell_{t}(M_{1:h})$ is convex in $M_{1:h}$ .

#### Proof.

The loss function $\ell_{t}$ is given by $\ell_{t}(M_{1:h})=c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}),\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h})).$ Since the cost $c_{t}$ is a convex function with respect to its arguments, we simply need to show that $\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M}$ depend linearly on $M_{1:h}$ . The state is given by

$$ \mathbf{x}_{t}^{M}=A\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{M}+B\mathbf{u}_{t-1}^{M}+\mathbf{w}_{t-1}=A\mathbf{x}_{t-1}^{M}+B\left(\sum_{i=1}^{h}\sigma_{i}^{1/4}M_{i}\tilde{W}_{t-2:t-m-1}\bm{\phi}_{i}\right)+\mathbf{w}_{t-1}\,. $$

By induction, we can further simplify

$$ \mathbf{x}_{t}^{M}=\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}M_{j}\tilde{W}_{t-i-1:t-i-m}\bm{\phi}_{j}\,, $$

which is a linear function of the variables. Similarly, the control $\mathbf{u}_{t}$ is given by

$$ \mathbf{u}_{t}^{M}=\sum_{i=1}^{h}\sigma_{i}^{1/4}M_{i}\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\bm{\phi}_{i}\,. $$

Thus, we have shown that $\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h})$ and $\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h})$ are linear transformations of $M_{1:h}$ . A composition of convex and linear functions is convex, which concludes our Lemma. ∎

### 6.2 Lipschitzness of $\ell_{t}(\cdot)$

The following lemma states and proves the explicit lipschitz constant of $\ell_{t}(\cdot)$ .

#### Lemma 6.3.

For any $M_{1:h},M^{\prime}_{1:h}\in{\mathcal{K}}$ it holds that,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\ell_{t}(M_{1:h})-\ell_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right|\leq\frac{6G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{5}W^{2}\sqrt{m}h}{\gamma^{2}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\left\lVert M_{1:h}-M_{1:h}^{\prime}\right\rVert\,. $$

#### Proof.

Taking the difference in controls:

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{u}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert=\left\lVert\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}(M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j})\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\phi_{j}\right\rVert\leq W\sqrt{m}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left\lVert M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert\,. $$

By unrolling the recursion, we have:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h})=\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}M_{j}\tilde{W}_{t-i-1:t-i-m}\phi_{j}\,, $$

Taking the difference,

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{x}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert \displaystyle=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}(M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j})\tilde{W}_{t-i-1:t-i-m}\phi_{j}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{t}\left\lVert A^{i-1}\right\rVert\left\lVert B\right\rVert\sum_{j=1}^{h}|\sigma_{j}|^{1/4}\left\lVert M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert\left\lVert\tilde{W}_{t-i-1:t-i-m}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{t}\kappa^{2}(1-\gamma)^{i-1}\kappa_{B}W\sqrt{m}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\right)\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left\lVert M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert \displaystyle\leq W\sqrt{m}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\left(\frac{\kappa^{2}\kappa_{B}}{\gamma}\right)\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left\lVert M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert\,. $$

Using the fact that $\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}/\gamma>1$ , we get a uniform bound:

$$ \displaystyle\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{x}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{u}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert\right\}\leq\frac{\kappa_{B}\kappa^{2}W\sqrt{m}}{\gamma}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left\lVert M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert\,. $$

Using the lipschizness of the cost function from Assumption 3.3, the definition of ${\mathcal{K}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\ell_{t}(M_{1:h})-\ell_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right| \displaystyle=\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}),\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h}))-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h}),\mathbf{u}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h}))\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{3G\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}\left(\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{x}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert+\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{u}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{6G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{5}W^{2}\sqrt{m}}{\gamma^{2}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\sum_{j=1}^{h}\left\lVert M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert\,. $$

Finally, we upper bound each $\left\lVert M_{j}-M^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert$ by $\left\lVert M_{1:h}-M^{\prime}_{1:h}\right\rVert$ to get the result.

∎

### 6.3 Loss functions with memory

The actual loss $c_{t}$ at time $t$ is not calculated on $\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})$ , but rather on the true state $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ , which in turn depends on different parameters $M_{1:h}^{i}$ for various historical times $i<t$ . Nevertheless, $c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})$ is well approximated by $\ell_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})$ , as stated in Lemma 4.5 and proven next.

Proof of Lemma 4.5: By the choice of step size $\eta$ , and by the computation of the lipschitz constant of $\ell_{t}$ w.r.t $M_{1:h}$ in Lemma 6.3, we have:

$$ \eta=\frac{2\kappa^{3}}{L}\sqrt{\frac{2h}{\gamma T}}\,, $$

where $L$ is the lipschitz constant of $\ell_{t}$ w.r.t $M_{1:h}$ , computed in Lemma 6.3. Thus, for each $j\in[h]$ ,

$$ \|M_{j}^{t}-M_{j}^{t-i}\|\leq\|M_{1:h}^{t}-M_{1:h}^{t-i}\|\leq\sum_{s=t-i+1}^{t}\|M_{1:h}^{s}-M_{1:h}^{s-1}\|\leq i\eta L=2i\kappa^{3}\sqrt{\frac{2h}{\gamma T}}\,. $$

Observe that $\mathbf{u}_{t}=\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})$ . We use the fact proved above to establish that $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})$ are close. Observe that $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})$ can be written as

$$ \mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}M_{j}^{t}\tilde{W}_{t-i-1:t-i-m}\bm{\phi}_{j}\,, $$

$$ \mathbf{x}_{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}+\sum_{i=1}^{t}A^{i-1}B\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}M_{j}^{t-i}\tilde{W}_{t-i-1:t-i-m}\bm{\phi}_{j}\,. $$

Evaluating the difference,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})\| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{t}\|A^{i-1}\|\|B\|\sum_{j=1}^{h}|\sigma_{j}|^{1/4}\|M_{j}^{t-i}-M_{j}^{t}\|\|\tilde{W}_{t-i-1:t-i-m}\| \displaystyle\leq 2\kappa^{5}\kappa_{B}W\sqrt{m}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2h}{\gamma T}}\sum_{i=1}^{t}i(1-\gamma)^{i-1} \displaystyle\leq\frac{2\kappa^{5}\kappa_{B}W\sqrt{mh}}{\gamma^{5/2}\sqrt{T}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\,. $$

By definition, $\ell_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})=c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t}),\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t}))$ , and by the definition of ${\mathcal{K}}$ and the projection used in Algorithm 1 we have by Assumption 3.3:

$$ \displaystyle\left|\ell_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})\right| \displaystyle=\left|c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t}),\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t}))-c_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t})\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{3G\kappa^{3}W}{\gamma}\|\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h}^{t})-\mathbf{x}_{t}\| \displaystyle\leq\frac{6G\kappa_{B}\kappa^{8}W^{2}\sqrt{mh}}{\gamma^{7/2}\sqrt{T}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\,. $$

$\square$

## 7 Spectral Tail Bounds

We use the following low-approximate rank property of positive semidefinite Hankel matrices, from Beckermann and Townsend (2016):

#### Lemma 7.1.

[Corollary 5.4 in Beckermann and Townsend (2016)] Let $H_{n}$ be a PSD Hankel matrix of dimension $n$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{j+2k}(H_{n})\leq 16\left[\exp\left(\frac{\pi^{2}}{4\log(8\lfloor n/2\rfloor/\pi)}\right)\right]^{-2k+2}\sigma_{j}(H_{n})\,. $$

Define the matrix

$$ \displaystyle H_{m}=\intop_{0}^{1-\gamma}\mu_{\alpha}\mu_{\alpha}^{\top}d\alpha\,, $$

where $\mu_{\alpha}=[1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{m-1}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$ , and note that $(H_{m})_{i,j}=\frac{(1-\gamma)^{i+j-1}}{i+j-1}$ . In particular, this is a PSD Hankel matrix of dimension $m$ . We prove the following additional properties related to it:

#### Lemma 7.2.

Let $\sigma_{j}$ be the $j^{\sf th}$ top singular value of $H_{m}$ . Then, for all $T\geq 10$ , we have

$$ \sigma_{j}\leq 156800\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}j}{4\log T}\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\,. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by noting that for any $j$ ,

$$ \sigma_{j}\leq\Tr(H_{m})=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\left(1-\gamma\right)^{2i-1}}{2i-1}\leq(1-\gamma)\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{(1-\gamma)^{2i}}{2i+1}=(1-\gamma)\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{2-\gamma}{\gamma}\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\,. $$

Now, since $T\geq 10$ implies $8\lfloor T/2\rfloor/\pi>T$ , we have by Lemma 7.1 that

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{2+2k}\leq\sigma_{1+2k} \displaystyle<8\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\cdot\left[\exp\left(\frac{\pi^{2}}{2\log T}\right)\right]^{-k+1} \displaystyle<1120\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}k}{2\log T}\right). $$

Thus, we have that for all $j$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{j}<1120\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}(j-2)}{2\log T}\right)<156800\log\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}j}{2\log T}\right)\,. $$

∎

#### Lemma 7.3.

For all $T\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0\leq\alpha\leq 1-\gamma$ , we have:

- 1. $\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}\leq 1/\gamma\,,$

- 2. $\left|\frac{d}{d\alpha}\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}\right|\leq 2/\gamma^{2}\,.$

#### Proof.

The first inequality can obtained by evaluating:

$$ \displaystyle\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha^{2i-2}=\frac{1-\alpha^{2m}}{1-\alpha^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{1-(1-\gamma)^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{\gamma}\,. $$

To obtain the second inequality, observe that in the summation form, $\left|\frac{d}{d\alpha}\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}\right|=\sum_{i=2}^{m}(2i-2)\alpha^{2i-3}$ and hence it monotonically increases with $m$ . Thus, if the limit exists for $\left|\frac{d}{d\alpha}\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}\right|$ as $m\rightarrow\infty$ then the limit is the supremum. Evaluating the derivative for the closed form expression of $\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}$ , and taking the supremum, we get:

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{d}{d\alpha}\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}\right| \displaystyle\leq\sup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\left|\frac{(-2m\alpha^{2m-1})(1-\alpha^{2})-(1-\alpha^{2m})(-2\alpha)}{(1-\alpha^{2})^{2}}\right| \displaystyle=\sup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\left|\frac{2\alpha-2m\alpha^{2m-1}+2m\alpha^{2m+1}-2\alpha^{2m+1}}{(1-\alpha^{2})^{2}}\right| \displaystyle=\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\left|\frac{2\alpha-2m\alpha^{2m-1}+2m\alpha^{2m+1}-2\alpha^{2m+1}}{(1-\alpha^{2})^{2}}\right| \displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha}{(1-\alpha^{2})^{2}}\leq\frac{2(1-\gamma)}{(1-(1-\gamma)^{2})^{2}}\leq\frac{2}{\gamma^{2}}\,. $$

∎

#### Lemma 7.4.

Let $\{\phi_{j}\}$ be the eigenvectors of $H_{m}$ . Then for all $j\in[T]$ , $\alpha\in[0,1-\gamma]$ , and $\gamma\leq 2/3$ ,

$$ |\mu_{\alpha}^{\top}\phi_{j}|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{\gamma}}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}\leq\frac{30}{\sqrt{\gamma}}\log^{1/4}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}j}{16\log T}\right)\,. $$

#### Proof.

Consider the scalar function $g(\alpha)=(\mu_{\alpha}^{\top}\phi_{j})^{2}$ over the interval $[0,1-\gamma]$ . First, notice that by definition of $\phi_{j}$ as the eigenvectors of $H_{m}$ , and $\sigma_{j}$ as the corresponding eigenvalues, we have

$$ \int_{0}^{1-\gamma}g(\alpha)d\alpha=\int_{0}^{1-\gamma}\big(\phi_{j}^{\top}\mu_{\alpha}\big)^{2}d\alpha=\int_{0}^{1-\gamma}\phi_{j}^{\top}\mu_{\alpha}\mu_{\alpha}^{\top}\phi_{j}d\alpha=\phi_{j}^{\top}Z_{h}\phi_{j}=\sigma_{j}. $$

Since $\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}$ is $2/\gamma^{2}$ -lipschitz in the interval $[0,1-\gamma]$ , and $g(\alpha)$ is its projection on $\phi_{j}$ , $g(\alpha)$ is also $2/\gamma^{2}$ -lipschitz. Note that $g(\alpha)$ is also a non-negative function and integrates to $\sigma_{j}$ over the interval $[0,1-\gamma]$ . Say $R$ is the maximum value achieved by $g(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha\in[0,1-\gamma]$ then $R\leq\left\lVert\mu_{\alpha}\right\rVert^{2}\leq 1/\gamma$ . Subject to achieveing the maximum at $R$ , the non-negative $2/\gamma^{2}$ -lipschitz function over $[0,1-\gamma]$ with the smallest integral is given by:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(\alpha)=\max\left\{R-\frac{2}{\gamma^{2}}\alpha,0\right\}\,, $$

for which $\int_{0}^{1-\gamma}\Delta(\alpha)d\alpha=R^{2}\gamma^{2}/4$ whenever $\gamma\leq 2/3$ . Thus, we get that $R\leq\frac{2}{\gamma}\sqrt{\sigma_{j}}$ and hence $|\mu_{\alpha}^{\top}\phi_{j}|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2}{\gamma}}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}$ . Using the upper bound on $\sigma_{j}$ from lemma 7.2, we get the result.

∎

## 8 Stabilized Spectral Policy

Assumption 3.5 restricts us to competing only against systems for which the zero matrix is $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -diagonalizably stable. This implies that there exists a decomposition:

$$ A=HLH^{-1}, $$

where $\|H\|,\|H^{-1}\|\leq\kappa$ , $L$ is diagonal, and $\|L\|\leq 1-\gamma$ . However, our proofs only require the bound:

$$ \forall\,\,i\in\mathbb{N},\quad\quad\quad\quad\|A^{i}\|\leq\kappa^{2}(1-\gamma)^{i}, $$

which holds even if $L$ is not diagonal. In fact, it suffices for the zero matrix to be $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -strongly stable, as defined in Cohen et al. (2018). For completeness, we recall the definition:

#### Definition 8.1 (Definition 3.1 in Cohen et al. (2018)).

A linear policy $K$ is $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -strongly stable if there exist matrices $L,H$ such that:

$$ A+BK=HLH^{-1}, $$

and the following conditions hold:

- 1. The spectral norm of $L$ is strictly smaller than unity, i.e., $\|L\|\leq 1-\gamma$ .

- 2. The controller and the transformation matrices are bounded, i.e., $\|K\|\,,\|H\|\,,\|H^{-1}\|\leq\kappa$ .

However, the assumption of $0$ being a $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -strongly stable linear controller can be further relaxed by using a precomputed $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -strongly stable matrix $K_{0}$ . This can be done using an $\sf SDP$ relaxation as described in Cohen et al. (2018). Given access to a $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -strongly stable $K_{0}$ , we learn a stabilized spectral policy using online gradient descent defined as follows:

$$ \mathbf{u}_{t}^{M}:=K_{0}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M}+\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sigma_{j}^{1/4}M_{j}\tilde{W}_{t-1:t-m}\bm{\phi}_{j}. $$

Consider playing $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}=\mathbf{u}_{t}+K_{0}\mathbf{x}_{t}$ instead of $\mathbf{u}_{t}$ at each $t\in[T]$ . Observe that the system

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=A\mathbf{x}_{t}+B\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}+\mathbf{w}_{t}\,, $$

when controlled by $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}$ behaves the same as the system

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=(A+BK_{0})\mathbf{x}_{t}+B\mathbf{u}_{t}+\mathbf{w}_{t}\,, $$

when controlled by $\mathbf{u}_{t}$ . This means that the sequence of states in both the cases is the same. Thus, since the $0$ matrix is a $(\kappa,\gamma)-$ strongly stable for system (8.2), the regret of our algorithm on system (8.2) is bounded by our result. By the structure of our proofs, for system (8.2), each one of

- (i) $\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}\right\rVert\right\}\,,$

- (ii) $\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}^{K,m}-\mathbf{x}_{t}^{M^{*}}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}-\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}}\right\rVert\right\}\,,$

- (iii) $\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{x}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}(M_{1:h})-\mathbf{u}_{t}(M^{\prime}_{1:h})\right\rVert\right\}\,,$

- (iv) $\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{x}_{t}(M^{t}_{1:h})\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}_{t}-\mathbf{u}_{t}(M^{t}_{1:h})\right\rVert\right\}\,,$

remains bounded. Observe for any state $\mathbf{x}$ and control $\mathbf{u}$ , if $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{u}+K_{0}\mathbf{x}$ then:

$$ \displaystyle\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{u}}-\tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}\right\rVert\right\}\leq\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}^{\prime}\right\rVert+\kappa\left\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right\rVert\right\}\leq 2\kappa\max\left\{\left\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right\rVert,\left\lVert\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}^{\prime}\right\rVert\right\}\,. $$

Thus, replacing $\mathbf{u}_{t}(M)$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}(M)$ in (iii) and (iv) yields the same bound with an additional factor of $2\kappa$ . Now, observe that $\mathbf{u}^{K}=K\mathbf{x}=K_{0}\mathbf{x}+(K-K_{0})\mathbf{x}=\tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{(K-K_{0})}$ . Define

$$ \tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}^{K,m}:=K_{0}\mathbf{x}_{t}+(K-K_{0})\sum_{i=1}^{m}(A+BK)^{i-1}\mathbf{w}_{t-i}\,, $$

and choose

$$ \tilde{M}^{*}_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{-1/4}(K-K_{0})H\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bm{\phi}_{i}^{\top}\bm{\mu}_{\alpha_{j}}e_{j}e_{j}^{\top}\right)H^{-1}\quad\quad\quad\quad\forall\,i\in[h]\,. $$

Now, replacing $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K}$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}^{(K-K_{0})}$ , $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{K,m}$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}^{K,m}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{t}^{M^{*}}$ with $\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{t}^{\tilde{M}^{*}}$ in (i) and (ii), we get the same bounds with an additional factor of $2\kappa$ . This allows us to conclude that, when competing against the same policy class $\mathcal{S}$ , we get an upper bound on the regret with the same order of growth with respect to $T$ and $1/\gamma$ .

## 9 Advantage of Smaller $\gamma$

Previous works require a stability margin of $\gamma=\Omega(1/polylog(T))$ to ensure an $O(polylog(T))$ running time. In contrast, this work shows that setting $\gamma=\Omega(1/T^{k})$ for $k\in(1,1/12)$ maintains sublinear regret while still guaranteeing an $O(polylog(T))$ running time. In this section, we construct an example demonstrating that choosing $\gamma=1/T^{k}$ for $k\in(0,1/12)$ results in significantly lower aggregate loss compared to $\gamma=1/polylog(T)$ . Consider a noiseless linear dynamical system with parameters $a,b\in\mathbb{R}$ , governed by the update equation:

$$ x_{t+1}=ax_{t}+bu_{t}\,. $$

The loss function at each time step is defined as:

$$ \forall\,t\in[T],\quad c_{t}(x,u)=\max\{-x,-1\}. $$

Since this is a scalar system, for sufficiently large $\kappa$ , the class of $(\kappa,\gamma)$ -diagonalizably stable controllers reduces to:

$$ S(\gamma)=\{k\in{\mathbb{R}}\,|\,0\leq a+bk\leq 1-\gamma\}\,. $$

If the initial state $x_{0}=1$ , then:

$$ \displaystyle\min_{k\in S(\gamma)}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},u_{t})=\min_{k\in S(\gamma)}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(-x_{t})=-\max_{k\in S(\gamma)}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(a+bk)^{t-1}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}(1-\gamma)^{t-1}=-\frac{1-(1-\gamma)^{T}}{\gamma}\,. $$

Using the fact that $0\leq 1-\gamma\leq e^{-\gamma}$ , we can upper and lower bound this expression as:

$$ -\frac{1}{\gamma}\leq\min_{k\in S(\gamma)}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},u_{t})\leq-\frac{1-e^{-\gamma T}}{\gamma}\,. $$

Using the lower bound,

$$ \min_{k\in S(1/polylog(T))}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},u_{t})\geq-polylog(T)\,, $$

and using the upper bound,

$$ \min_{k\in S(1/T^{k})}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},u_{t})\leq-T^{k}(1-e^{-T^{(1-k)}})\leq-T^{k}/2\,. $$

Hence, the difference in the minimum costs of the two cases is lower bounded as:

$$ \min_{k\in S(1/polylog(T))}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},u_{t})-\min_{k\in S(1/T^{k})}\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{t}(x_{t},u_{t})\geq T^{k}/2-polylog(T)=\Omega(T^{k/2})\,. $$

Thus, choosing $\gamma=1/T^{k}$ results in a significantly lower cost for the best controller in the policy class $S(\gamma)$ (which we compete against) compared to the case when $\gamma=1/polylog(T)$ . In particular, the improvement is by a polynomial factor in $T$ .

## 10 Experiments

We present a series of synthetic experiments designed to evaluate the performance of Algorithm 1 (OSC). We compare OSC against the gradient perturbation controller (GPC) as defined in Agarwal et al. (2019a). We analyze the performance of both controllers under three different system settings: linear signal, where the initial state $\mathbf{x}_{0}$ is sampled from the Gaussian distribution; signal with the ReLU state transition; and the STU signal as outlined in Agarwal et al. (2024b).

For each experiment setting, we consider an LDS with a state dimension of $d=100$ and a control dimension of $n=40$ . The system matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ is diagonalizable, with largest eigenvalue being $0.9$ , ensuring marginal stability. The control matrix $B\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ consists of Normally distributed entries.

Figure 2 shows that the OSC controller with reduced number of parameters outperforms the GPC controller under all signal settings.

## 11 Conclusion and Discussion

We presented a new method for online control of linear dynamical systems under adversarial disturbances and cost functions. While inspired by ideas from spectral filtering in online prediction, our approach introduces a fundamentally different relaxation tailored to the control setting, where past responses are not directly observed and actions shape future trajectories. By approximating linear policies using spectral filters derived from a specific Hankel matrix, we construct a convex relaxation that enables efficient online learning.

Our approach achieves logarithmic dependence on the inverse of the stability margin, resulting in exponentially faster runtime and fewer learnable parameters, while maintaining optimal regret guarantees. More broadly, our technique offers a new perspective on approximating linear policies for control and may be of independent interest beyond the setting studied here.

# The Quasiparticle Ansatz for Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product States

## Abstract

The Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product State (RCMPS) ansatz introduced in [1] is a translation-invariant variational ansatz intended to approximate the ground states of gapped one-dimensional relativistic Quantum Field Theories directly in the continuum limit and in infinite volume. In this work, we develop an ansatz, referred to as the Relativistic Quasiparticle (RQP) ansatz, for the low-lying one-particle excitations of the RCMPS vacuum, as well as for solitons interpolating between two distinct degenerate vacua. The corresponding energies of these states can be obtained as the eigenvalues of an effective Hamiltonian. The RQP ansatz generalizes constructions used in the Matrix Product State and Continuous Matrix Product State literature. We apply the RQP ansatz to the sine-Gordon model and find good agreement with results from integrability for both the soliton and breather masses. We also apply the RQP ansatz to the $\phi^{4}$ theory, in both its $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ -preserving and $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ -broken phases, and determine the spectrum of particles and solitons. This enables us to determine the parameter regime for which multiple stable particles exist.

## 1 Introduction

Matrix Product States (MPSs) [2] and Hamiltonian lattice methods have become increasingly important tools in understanding strongly coupled dynamics in $(1+1)$ d quantum field theories (QFTs) (see [3, 4, 5] for reviews). MPSs are ansätze for many-body wave functions of lattice systems that exhibit area law entanglement entropy, which make them efficient approximations of gapped ground states. MPS methods have been used to study gauge theories with fermionic matter [6, 7, 8], scalar field theories [9], conformal field theories [10, 11], and, importantly, an array of real-time observables [12, 13]. Furthermore, the MPS ansatz can be extended to model excitations using the quasiparticle ansatz [14] and estimate bound state masses in the aforementioned models [8, 15]. Since MPSs are formulated on a spatial lattice, the quantum dynamics is governed by a lattice Hamiltonian that approximates the continuum one as the lattice spacing is taken to zero. Fermionic theories are especially well-suited for such numerical lattice studies because the fermion statistics naturally yields a finite local Hilbert space at each lattice site. Moreover, in $(1+1)$ d, one can avoid some of the fermion doubling that plagues higher dimensional lattice theories. On the other hand, lattice realizations of bosonic theories exhibit infinite-dimensional local Hilbert spaces that must be truncated in numerical implementations. This truncation introduces an additional cutoff, and one needs to make sure that the low-energy observables of interest converge as one increases the truncation parameter [9].

An elegant way of dispensing with the lattice is the Continuous Matrix Product State (CMPS) introduced in [16], which formulates an ansatz analogous to the discrete MPS for a non-relativistic QFT directly in the continuum limit. Using the CMPS ansatz, the issue of finiteness of local Hilbert spaces in bosonic theories does not arise since, in continuous space, multiple occupancy is equivalent to single occupancy of infinitesimally neighboring points [16]. CMPSs have been applied to both fermionic and bosonic relativistic QFTs, but they require the introduction of explicit counterterms for the ground state search to converge [17, 10]. For the case of scalar field theories with non-derivative interactions, this situation is somewhat unsatisfying, as it is well known that such theories can be rendered finite by normal-ordering [18]. This issue was addressed more recently in [1] with the introduction of Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product States (RCMPSs), which adapt CMPSs to relativistic scalar field theories making the ultraviolet (UV) finiteness manifest. The key insight of RCMPSs is to employ a basis of states derived from the energy eigenstates of the free massive scalar field theory. RCMPSs automatically encode properties of relativistic QFT such as the short-distance behavior of two-point functions, making them better starting points for approximating interacting vacua. The RCMPS framework allows for efficient simulation of ground state properties directly in the continuum limit and at infinite volume. The method was initially used to study $\phi^{4}$ theory [1] and later the sine-Gordon and sinh-Gordon models [19], defect QFTs [20], the $O(2)$ model [21]. This framework was also used to constrain the spectral density through vacuum correlators [22].

The RCMPS ansatz has the same structure as the CMPS ansatz, so it is natural to attempt to adapt CMPS constructions to the language of RCMPS. One such construction is the quasiparticle ansatz [23], which models a single particle- or soliton-like excitation as a local perturbation of a vacuum state as encoded by a CMPS. The quasiparticle ansatz was used to determine the dispersion of particles in non-relativistic QFTs but has, to the best of our knowledge, not been applied to relativistic systems. On the other hand, the quasiparticle ansatz for MPSs has proved to be a powerful tool in determining excitation spectra in relativistic gauge theories [8, 24, 15].

In this work, we adapt the quasiparticle ansatz to RCMPSs, which we will refer to as Relativistic Quasiparticle (RQP) ansatz. The RQP ansatz allows us to study both the spectrum of particle-like excitations as well as solitons of $(1+1)$ d scalar QFTs. We first apply the RQP ansatz to the sine-Gordon model, which is integrable [25] and exhibits a rich spectrum of particles and solitons whose masses are known exactly. The numerical results from the RQP ansatz are in good agreement with integrability results. Furthermore, we find that the RQP ansatz accurately reproduces the relativistic dispersion relation required by the Lorentz invariance of the QFT. This agreement demonstrates that RCMPSs and the RQP ansatz are good approximations of relativistic states despite neither of them being manifestly relativistic.

We also apply the RQP ansatz to the $\phi^{4}$ theory. As the coupling is taken from weak to strong, this theory undergoes a phase transition that belongs to the Ising universality class [26]. We observe that the mass gap closes at a value of the coupling that is in agreement with other estimates in the literature [27]. The RQP ansatz gives full access to the spectrum of particles and solitons, and it can be used to determine for which parameters stable excitations can exist. In particular, we find that deep in the strong coupling/ $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ -broken phase, the spectrum contains two stable particles and a soliton (and associated anti-soliton), in agreement with semi-classical predictions and earlier numerical evidence [28, 29, 30].

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the RCMPS ansatz and how to use it to compute expectation values in scalar field theories. In Section 3, we define the RQP ansatz and derive the necessary formulas to determine the spectrum of particles and solitons. The formalism is applied in Section 4 to the sine-Gordon and $\phi^{4}$ theories. Technical details are contained in the Appendices.

## 2 Relativistic Continuous Matrix Product States

We begin by reviewing the RCMPS ansatz and establishing notation and formalism that will serve as the basis for the derivation of the RQP ansatz.

### 2.1 The RCMPS ansatz

RCMPSs were first introduced in [1] for studying relativistic $(1+1)$ -dimensional field theories with a single scalar field $\phi$ and non-derivative interactions. Such theories have Lagrangian and Hamiltonian densities of the form11 1 We denote the coordinates by $x^{\mu}=(t,x)$ , and we use the Minkowski metric $\eta_{\mu\nu}=\text{diag}\,\{1,-1\}$ to raise and lower space-time indices.

$$ {\cal L}=\frac{1}{2}\dot{\phi}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}-V(\phi)\,,\qquad{\cal H}=\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+V(\phi)\,, $$

where $V(\phi)$ is the scalar potential and $\pi=\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial\dot{\phi}}$ is the canonical momentum conjugate to $\phi$ . We may assume that $V(\phi)$ has a global minimum at $\phi=0$ where $V(0)=0$ , so that

$$ V(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2}+V_{\text{int}}(\phi)\,, $$

where $m$ is the mass of the field $\phi$ around the $\phi=0$ vacuum and $V_{\text{int}}(\phi)$ is the interaction potential, whose Taylor series expansion around $\phi=0$ is assumed to start at cubic order. The methods we will develop have general applicability to potentials that can be expressed as sums of polynomials and exponentials in $\phi$ , with the concrete applications presented in Section 4 being restricted to the $\phi^{4}$ and sine-Gordon theories, for which

$$ \begin{split}\text{$\phi^{4}$ theory:}&\qquad V_{\phi^{4}}(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2}+g\phi^{4}\,,\\
\text{sine-Gordon theory:}&\qquad V_{\text{sG}}(\phi)=\frac{m^{2}}{\beta^{2}}\left[1-\cos(\beta\phi)\right]\,.\end{split} $$

The two examples (2.3) consist of families of theories parameterized by the dimensionless parameters $g/m^{2}$ in the $\phi^{4}$ case and $\beta$ in the sine-Gordon case22 2 The mass parameter $m$ serves only as a renormalization scale as will be explained in Section 4.1.

At the quantum level, the precise definition of the field theory (2.1) requires more care. To be specific, we will work in the Schrödinger picture, where both $\phi$ and $\pi$ are time-independent quantum operators obeying

$$ [\phi(x),\pi(y)]=i\delta(x-y)\,. $$

Since $V(\phi)$ is a composite operator, it requires regularization. A standard procedure in $(1+1)$ -dimensional QFTs without irrelevant interactions is to use a normal ordering prescription with respect to a free scalar field of some mass $\mu$ .33 3 The parameter $\mu$ used for normal ordering is not necessarily equal to the mass $m$ mentioned above. (Different choices of $\mu$ correspond to different regularization prescriptions.) As usual, the normal order product $N_{\mu}[\cdots]$ of any number of $\phi$ and $\pi$ operators is defined by expanding these operators in Fourier modes of a free scalar field of mass $\mu$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\phi(x) \displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\omega_{k}}}(e^{ikx}a_{k}+e^{-ikx}a_{k}^{\dagger})\,, \displaystyle\pi(x) \displaystyle=-i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\omega_{k}}{2}}(e^{ikx}a_{k}-e^{-ikx}a_{k}^{\dagger})\,, $$

with $\omega_{k}\equiv\sqrt{\mu^{2}+k^{2}}$ , and then ordering the $a_{k}$ and $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ operators under the $N_{\mu}$ sign such that all $a_{k}$ appear to the right of all $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ . Normal ordering then provides a precise definition of our theory whereby the dynamics is given by the Hamiltonian

$$ H=\int dx\,\mathcal{H}\,,\qquad{\cal H}\equiv N_{\mu}\left[\frac{1}{2}\pi^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+V(\phi)\right]\,. $$

Note the normal ordering $N_{\mu}[\cdots]$ distinguishes the Fock vacuum $|0\rangle$ as the state annihilated by all of the annihilation operators, $a_{k}|0\rangle=0$ . This state is the ground state for the specific case $V(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}\phi^{2}$ .

Regardless of the value of $\mu$ , the commutation relations (2.4) imply $[a_{k},a_{k^{\prime}}]=[a_{k}^{\dagger},a_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger}]=0$ and $[a_{k},a_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger}]=2\pi\delta(k-k^{\prime})$ , which, in turn, imply that the Fourier transforms of $a_{k}$ and $a_{k}^{\dagger}$ ,

$$ a(x)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\,e^{ikx}a_{k}\,,\qquad a^{\dagger}(x)\equiv\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dk}{2\pi}\,e^{-ikx}a_{k}^{\dagger}\,, $$

obey the commutation relations

$$ [a(x),a(y)]=[a^{\dagger}(x),a^{\dagger}(y)]=0\,,\qquad[a(x),a^{\dagger}(y)]=\delta(x-y)\,. $$

The commutation relations (2.8) are identical to those of a non-relativistic (complex) scalar field $\psi(x)$ :

$$ [\psi(x),\psi(y)]=[\psi^{\dagger}(x),\psi^{\dagger}(y)]=0\,,\qquad[\psi(x),\psi^{\dagger}(y)]=\delta(x-y)\,. $$

Of course, $a(x)$ defined in (2.7) should not be interpreted as a non-relativistic scalar field.44 4 The interpretation of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$ is that, in the free theory $V(\phi)=\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}\phi^{2}$ , the operator $a^{\dagger}(x)$ creates a single quantum of the field $\phi$ localized within a region centered at $x$ whose size is comparable to the Compton wavelength $\sim\mu^{-1}$ , and the operator $a(x)$ annihilates such a quantum. Nevertheless, the fact that the equations (2.8) and (2.9) are identical allows one to consider an analog of the CMPS ansatz introduced in [16] for non-relativistic field theories by simply replacing $\psi\to a$ in many of the equations in [16]. The result is the RCMPS ansatz introduced in [1], which we now review.

For QFTs defined on the entire real line, the RCMPS is a translation-invariant ansatz that can be used to approximate the ground state. It is parameterized by two complex $\chi\times\chi$ constant matrices $Q,R$ , and two complex $\chi$ -dimensional vectors $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ :

$$ |Q,R\rangle=V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\mathcal{P}\exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\Bigl(Q\otimes\mathds{1}+R\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\Bigr)\right]V_{-\infty}|0\rangle\,. $$

Here, the tensor product is between the $\chi$ -dimensional virtual space on which $Q,R$ act and the physical Hilbert space of the QFT, the path ordered exponential $\mathcal{P}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,(\cdots)}$ is defined such that the operators with larger $x$ labels appear to the left of those with smaller $x$ labels, and the vectors $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ serve as boundary conditions for the virtual space of the path-ordered exponential. The parameter $\chi$ is known as the bond dimension, and it serves as the truncation parameter of the ansatz. As we will explain shortly, the matrices $Q$ , $R$ and the boundary vectors $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ must obey certain conditions in order for the state (2.10) to be normalized. Furthermore, as we will explain, the precise choices of $V_{+\infty},V_{-\infty}$ do not affect any physical quantities computed in infinite volume.

Note that one can also construct other variants of RCMPSs. One such variant that will be very useful in the following discussion consists of the more general family of states

$$ |{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle=V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\mathcal{P}\exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\Bigl({\bf Q}(x)\otimes\mathds{1}+{\bf R}(x)\otimes a^{\dagger}(x)\Bigr)\right]V_{-\infty}|0\rangle\,, $$

where ${\bf Q}(x)$ and ${\bf R}(x)$ are non-trivial functions of $x$ . Other generalizations of RCMPSs can be obtained by considering compact spaces and boundaries [31, 20].

### 2.2 Normalization conditions

To determine the conditions obeyed by $Q$ , $R$ , $V_{+\infty}$ , $V_{-\infty}$ for the RCMPS (2.10) to be normalized, we use the fact that the more general states (2.11) have the overlap (see Appendix A.1 for a proof)

$$ \begin{split}\langle\mathbf{Q}^{\prime},\mathbf{R}^{\prime}|\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{R}\rangle&=(V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\otimes V_{+\infty}^{\prime T})\mathcal{P}\exp\left[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\Bigl(\mathbf{Q}(x)\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\prime}(x)+\mathbf{R}(x)\otimes\overline{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}(x)\Bigr)\right]\\
&{}\times(V_{-\infty}\otimes\overline{V}^{\prime}_{-\infty})\,,\end{split} $$

where the tensor product is between $\mathbb{C}^{\chi}$ and $\overline{\mathbb{C}}^{\chi}$ . Taking $\mathbf{Q}(x)=\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}(x)=Q$ , $\mathbf{R}(x)=\mathbf{R}^{\prime}(x)=R$ , and $V^{\prime}_{\pm\infty}=V_{\pm\infty}$ gives

$$ \langle Q,R|Q,R\rangle=\left(v_{+\infty}\middle|\exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\mathbb{T}\right)\middle|v_{-\infty}\right)\,, $$

where we defined the transfer matrix $\mathbb{T}$ and the boundary vectors $|v_{-\infty})$ , $(v_{+\infty}|$ :

$$ \mathbb{T}\equiv Q\otimes\mathds{1}+\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{Q}+R\otimes\overline{R}\,,\qquad(v_{+\infty}|\equiv V_{+\infty}^{\dagger}\otimes V_{+\infty}^{T}\qquad|v_{-\infty})\equiv V_{-\infty}\otimes\overline{V}_{-\infty}\,, $$

and we removed the path ordering symbol since the matrix appearing in the integrand of the exponent is $x$ -independent.

The factor $e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\mathbb{T}}$ can be interpreted as the limit

$$ \exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\mathbb{T}\right)=\lim_{L\to\infty}e^{L\mathbb{T}}\,, $$

and it can be evaluated using the spectral decomposition of the $\chi^{2}\times\chi^{2}$ matrix $\mathbb{T}$ . Let $\lambda_{k}$ , $k=1,\ldots,\chi^{2}$ be the eigenvalues, and $|r_{k})$ and $(l_{k}|$ the right- and left-eigenvectors, obeying the eigenvalue equations

$$ \mathbb{T}|r_{k})=\lambda_{k}|r_{k})\,,\qquad(l_{k}|\mathbb{T}=(l_{k}|\lambda_{k}\,. $$

The eigenvectors of $\mathbb{T}$ can be chosen to be orthonormal, i.e. $(l_{k}|r_{k^{\prime}})=\delta_{kk^{\prime}}$ , but the left- and right-eigenvectors are in general not related to each other by Hermitian conjugation. As shown in [31] in the case of CMPSs55 5 Technically, the (R)CMPS has to be “injective” for this result to hold (see [31]). However, a generic (R)CMPS is injective, so it will have this property., for matrices $\mathbb{T}$ of the form (2.14), the eigenvalue with the largest real part (also referred to as the dominant eigenvalue) is unique and purely real. Let us take this eigenvalue to correspond to $k=1$ , and simply denote it by $\lambda$ and its corresponding eigenvectors by $|r)$ and $(l|$ . Using the spectral decomposition $\mathbb{T}=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}|r_{k})(l_{k}|$ , it then follows that $e^{L\mathbb{T}}=\sum_{k}e^{L\lambda_{k}}|r_{k})(l_{k}|\approx e^{L\lambda}|r)(l|$ for $L\to\infty$ . As we can see, the factor $e^{L\mathbb{T}}$ that we need to evaluate does not have a finite limit as $L\to\infty$ unless $\lambda=0$ . We therefore choose the $Q,R$ matrices such that $\lambda=0$ ,66 6 Such a choice can be easily made: from any given pair of matrices $(Q,R)$ for which the dominant eigenvalue $\lambda$ does not necessarily vanish, one can construct the new pair $(Q^{\prime},R^{\prime})=(Q-\frac{\lambda}{2}\mathds{1},R)$ for which the dominant eigenvalue vanishes. in which case $e^{L\mathbb{T}}$ approaches the projector $|r)(l|$ as $L\to\infty$ ,

$$ e^{L\mathbb{T}}\approx|r)(l|\qquad\text{for $L\to\infty$.} $$

Thus, from (2.13), we infer that the RCMPS is normalized provided that

$$ \langle Q,R|Q,R\rangle=({v}_{+\infty}|r)\times(l|v_{-\infty})=1\,. $$

This is a condition that must be obeyed by the boundary vectors $V_{\pm\infty}$ . For future convenience, we will further restrict these boundary vectors such that each factor in (2.18) equals one separately:

$$ \displaystyle\left(v_{+\infty}\middle|r\right)=1\,,\qquad\left(l\middle|v_{-\infty}\right)=1. $$

To summarize, we restrict the parameters $Q$ , $R$ such that the largest eigenvalue of the transfer matrix (2.14) is $\lambda=0$ , which implies that the corresponding eigenvectors obey

$$ \mathbb{T}|r)=(l|\mathbb{T}=0\,,\qquad(l|r)=1\,, $$

and we furthermore restrict $V_{\pm\infty}$ such that the conditions (2.19) are satisfied. These conditions ensure that the RCMPS is normalized.

### 2.3 Matrix notation and RCMPS gauge redundancy

To further characterize the zero-eigenvectors $(l|$ and $|r)$ , it is convenient to interpret these eigenvectors as $\chi\times\chi$ matrices. Such an identification is possible because the matrix $\mathbb{T}$ acts (on the right) on vectors $|u)\in\mathbb{C}^{\chi}\otimes\overline{\mathbb{C}}^{\chi}$ and on the left on co-vectors $(w|\in\overline{\mathbb{C}}^{\chi}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{\chi}$ . From the components of $|u)$ and $(w|$ we can build the components $u_{i}{}^{j}$ and $w_{i}{}^{j}$ of the matrices $u$ and $w$ using the standard rule for Kronecker products

$$ |u)_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ \cong\ u_{i}{}^{j}\,,\qquad(w|_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ \cong\ [w^{\dagger}]_{j}{}^{i}\,,\qquad i,j=1,\ldots,\chi\,. $$

In this notation, the inner product and the action of an operator of the form $A\otimes B$ become

$$ \begin{split}(w|u)\ &\cong\ \tr(w^{\dagger}u)\,,\\
[A\otimes\overline{B}|u)]_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ &\cong\ [AuB^{\dagger}]_{i}{}^{j}\,,\\
[(w|A\otimes\overline{B}]_{(i-1)\chi+j}\ &\cong\ [B^{\dagger}w^{\dagger}A]_{j}{}^{i}\,.\end{split} $$

We can then write the eigenvalue equations (2.20) as

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{T}|r) \displaystyle=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad Qr+rQ^{\dagger}+RrR^{\dagger}=0\,, \displaystyle(l|\mathbb{T} \displaystyle=0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad Q^{\dagger}l+lQ+R^{\dagger}lR=0\,. $$

The structure of the transfer matrix (2.23) furthermore guarantees that the fixed points $r$ and $l$ are positive definite matrices [31] and, in particular, Hermitian.

The RCMPS ansatz is overparameterized in the sense that the transformation

$$ Q\rightarrow XQX^{-1}\,,\qquad R\rightarrow XRX^{-1} $$

does not change the physical state for any invertible matrix $X$ .77 7 From the definition (2.10), it is clear that this gauge transformation should be accompanied by a transformation of the boundary vectors $V_{\pm\infty}$ for the state to be invariant. However, since the boundary vectors do not change bulk observables, we can safely ignore their transformation. We can use this redundancy to trivialize the left or right fixed point [31] i.e. set $l=\mathds{1}$ or $r=\mathds{1}$ , respectively. In this work, we will do the former and use

$$ \text{{left-gauge}:}\qquad l=\mathds{1}\,, $$

which implies that the right fixed point satisfies $\tr(r)=1$ , as per the normalization condition $(l|r)=\tr(lr)=1$ . The choice $l=\mathds{1}$ further constrains the matrices $Q,R$ through (2.23)

$$ Q^{\dagger}+Q+R^{\dagger}R=0\,, $$

which fixes the Hermitian part of $Q$ in terms of $R^{\dagger}R$ .

### 2.4 Generating functional for correlators of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$

Having defined the states $|Q,R\rangle$ , we would now like to compute expectation values of various (normal-ordered) operators in these states, most importantly of the Hamiltonian density ${\cal H}$ . All normal-ordered operators can be written in terms of normal-ordered products of $a(x)$ and $a^{\dagger}(x)$ , so the first step is to compute a generating functional for such products:

$$ \mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]\equiv\left\langle Q,R\middle|N_{\mu}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\left(\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)+j(x)a(x)\right)}\right]\middle|Q,R\right\rangle\,, $$

where $\tilde{\jmath}$ and $j$ are classical sources, which, for simplicity, we assume to have compact support. Since

$$ N_{\mu}\left[e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\left(\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)+j(x)a(x)\right)}\right]=e^{-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\tilde{\jmath}(x)j(x)}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,j(x)a(x)}e^{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\tilde{\jmath}(x)a^{\dagger}(x)}\,, $$

we can relate (2.27) to the overlap of two generalized RCMPSs that were defined in (2.11):

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j] \displaystyle=e^{-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,\tilde{\jmath}(x)j(x)}\langle{\bf Q}^{\prime},{\bf R}^{\prime}|{\bf Q},{\bf R}\rangle\,, $$

with ${\bf Q}^{\prime}(x)={\bf Q}(x)=Q$ , ${\bf R}^{\prime}(x)=R+\overline{j}(x)\mathds{1}$ , and ${\bf R}(x)=R+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}$ , and with identical boundary vectors at both ends, $V_{\pm\infty}^{\prime}=V_{\pm\infty}$ . Now the expression for the generating functional follows directly from (2.12):

$$ \mathcal{Z}[\tilde{\jmath},j]=\left(v_{+\infty}\middle|\mathcal{P}\exp\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dx\,[\mathbb{T}+j(x)R\otimes\mathds{1}+\tilde{\jmath}(x)\mathds{1}\otimes\overline{R}]\right)\middle|v_{-\infty}\right)\,, $$
